claim: AGM belief revision is a normative, idealised theory (closed belief sets, logical omniscience). Revision reduces to contraction (Levi identity), and the theory does not say which belief to drop; an entrenchment or selection order must be supplied from outside.
agent_test: Compare S5 with an explicit ranked list of candidate claims (entrenchment taken from check evidence) versus unranked revise-everything; equal tokens; count wrong-belief retentions.
audit_note: SEP (Hansson) covers closed belief sets/logical omniscience as an idealisation, the Levi identity, and the need for selection functions or entrenchment; Almeida and Casals survey independently states the same points (Levi identity, logical omniscience, selection function/entrenchment). The five SEP entries are one source.

claim: Belief bases (finite stated lists) with Relevance replace closed sets plus Recovery in practice (SEP); at least one agent-memory system (Kumiho) rejects Recovery on purpose, and a recent agent paper (Chowdhury 2026) keeps AGM-style postulates but claims no representation theorem.
agent_test: Keep the candidate set as an explicit base with provenance; ablate closure (no re-derivation of consequences) and check for no loss on a revise-heavy task.
audit_note: Only one agent-memory system (Park's Kumiho) is shown rejecting Recovery on purpose, not several 'builders'; Chowdhury adopts AGM-style postulates and disclaims a representation theorem, which fits 'keep the postulates, drop the machinery' but is a single paper.
claim_before_audit: Belief bases (finite stated lists) with Relevance replace closed sets plus Recovery in practice; Recovery is rejected on purpose by agent-memory builders, and recent agent papers keep the postulates but drop the full machinery.

claim: Iterated revision needs extra postulates (Darwiche-Pearl C1-C4); lexicographic revision is the least conservative admissible operator, restrained revision the most conservative; the choice of operator is open.
agent_test: Test two policies on repeated failing checks: latest evidence always outranks all earlier (lexicographic) versus move only the minimum (restrained); measure oscillation and final accuracy.
audit_note: SEP names the postulates DP1-DP4 (C1-C4 in the original); Booth and Meyer state lexicographic is least and restrained most conservative among admissible operators; the arXiv and JAIR entries are one paper and the two Aravanis entries are one paper.

claim: AGM Success and Vacuity are contested when beliefs are about beliefs or when the input is itself uncertain; one observation need not force acceptance.
agent_test: Inject a single noisy failing check; compare always-accept with accept-only-after-a-re-run-confirms; measure false revisions.

claim: People do not follow minimal change and tend to give up the general conditional before the specific fact. Elio and Pelletier (1997, independent lab) found conditionals abandoned more than ground facts and no match to four formal minimal-change definitions; Vasileiou et al. (2025, N=62/60/60) found 83.37%, 85.51% and 67.16% non-minimal revisions; Walsh and Johnson-Laird (2009) found 17 of 20 revising the conditional (p<.01). Whether explanation causes the choice rests on one lab (see K22).
agent_test: Do not hard-code minimal change as the drop rule; compare dropping the lowest-provenance contradicting claim with dropping the fewest claims, at equal tokens. Human data say what people do, not what is best for an agent.
audit_note: Walsh and Johnson-Laird 17 of 20 (p<.01) and Vasileiou 83.37/85.51/67.16 percent non-minimal (N=62/60/60) verified; Elio and Pelletier verified from abstract/record only (full text not opened).

claim: LLMs revise poorly when a premise defeats a conclusion. On Belief-R (about 30 models, 1744 three-premise items: 1074 update, 670 maintain), small and open models score near 0% on update and large models reach at most about 50% on the mean of update and maintain (BREU). Strong maintainers are weak updaters and the reverse (GPT-4 Turbo 19.65/82.69; Mixtral 8x22B 35.38/36.57).
agent_test: Run Belief-R style items with and without a forced step asking whether the new fact removes a needed condition, at equal tokens; report BU and BM separately, never only the mean.

claim: Chain of thought and plan-and-solve do not repair belief revision in zero-shot prompting; mean gain is about 1 BREU point, and effects differ in sign by model.
agent_test: Compare a plain prompt with a revise-specific structured step; thinking longer alone is not a fix.

claim: Models keep stale answers after a premise edit (inertia): Qwen3-1.7B 0.667 initial to 0.467 revised, inertia 0.600 (n=30); Qwen3-4B 0.650 to 0.450, inertia 0.600 (n=20); Phi-4-mini 0.950 to 0.850. Other benchmarks (DERELAB, STALE, BeliefShift, Belief-R, ClawArena) report staleness or anchoring too. DeltaLogic samples are tiny and the models are small.
agent_test: Insert a defeating edit mid-task; measure how often the old answer survives, with and without an explicit re-derive-from-current-evidence state.
audit_note: DeltaLogic numbers match (Qwen3-1.7B 0.667/0.467/0.600 n=30; Qwen3-4B 0.650/0.450/0.600 n=20; Phi-4-mini 0.950/0.850; the four DeltaLogic entries are one paper); DERELAB (anchoring), STALE (outdated-memory failures) and BeliefShift (models miss legitimate updates) corroborate; ClawArena not opened.

claim: Models recognise staleness better than they act on it: DERELAB GPT-5-mini labels weakening turns right 95.4% but entailment accuracy is 20.3%; STALE state resolution 76.0% vs policy adaptation 39.0% (Qwen3.5-27B); premise resistance mostly under 5%.
agent_test: After detecting a stale claim, force a write step that lists dependent claims and re-checks them; measure downstream answer correctness.
audit_note: DERELAB (GPT-5-mini C2-eff 95.4 vs C2 acc 20.3) and STALE (Qwen3.5-27B Type I SR 76.0 vs IPA 39.0) verified; 'premise resistance mostly under 5 percent' holds for most systems but not all (Gemini-3.1-pro reaches 30.0 on Type I PR).

claim: Without outside feedback, asking an LLM to revise its own answer does not help and often hurts; with an oracle correctness label it helps (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3; GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0). Reliable external feedback or the true error location is what makes revision work. Added 2023-2026 checks: at equal budget self-repair was 1.05x and 0.97x of resampling (GPT-4, APPS); human feedback gave 52.6% repair success vs 33.3% for the model's own feedback; model-made location hints lowered correction for 2 of 3 models (Li 2026).
agent_test: Revise only when a real execution or checker output contradicts; compare with self-critique-triggered revision at equal tokens.
audit_note: Huang oracle table (75.9 to 84.3; 49.0 to 59.0), Olausson (1.05x with 10+1 allocation, 0.97x with 2+10 allocation; human feedback 33.3 to 52.6 percent) and Li 2026 (hints lower correction for GPT-3.5 and Claude, not DeepSeek) all verified.

claim: A bare challenge (Are you sure?) makes models flip answers: 46% flips on average and 17% mean accuracy drop over 10 LLMs and 7 tasks. Revision must be triggered by evidence, not by pressure.
agent_test: Add a content-free challenge in the loop; the agent should keep its best-so-far unless new evidence arrives.
audit_note: Laban et al. (FlipFlop): ten LLMs, seven tasks, flip 46 percent of the time, average accuracy drop 17 percent, verified; BeliefScope corroborates that pressure and evidence both move outputs. The closing sentence is a prescriptive conclusion.

claim: Given both memory and counter-evidence, LLMs favour their own memory (confirmation-like), more so for popular facts, and are order-sensitive (Llama2-7B 33.3 vs 82.8 by order); given only coherent counter-evidence they mostly accept it.
agent_test: Shuffle the order of the conflicting items in the revise prompt; measure decision variance.
audit_note: Xie et al.: models favor parametric memory when both are present, stronger for popular entities, and order-sensitive (Llama2-7B PopQA 33.3 vs 82.8 memorization ratio); counter-evidence alone accepted when coherent. DeReLab only supports the general confirmation-bias point.

claim: Weight editing is not belief revision: edited facts are stored but implied facts do not change (downstream accuracy 0.97 to 0.01 when it should change; MAE 0.34 to 0.59) and multi-hop questions fail. Putting edits in context or in external memory works better (in-context beats ROME by 10 to 29 points; MeLLo 85-91 on MQuAKE-T).
agent_test: Keep revised claims in an external visible ledger re-read each step rather than relying on the model to carry the edit.
audit_note: Numbers match (Hase Table 4: 0.97 to 0.01, MAE 0.34 to 0.59, on a synthetic-world model; Cohen ICE beats ROME by >10 (GPT-Neo) and 29 (LLaMA); MeLLo 85.5-91.1 on MQuAKE-T holds only for GPT-3.5, GPT-J/Vicuna are much lower).

claim: Structure beats per-item asking: classifying the revision once and propagating through a dependency graph by code recovers 1.00 of oracle savings (0.90 when paraphrased), versus 0.44 for asking a model node by node. Evidence is a single author-built benchmark. Related but not replications: dependency links raised step-error identification 3 to 14 points (PARC, 607 chains), and DeFA's dependency graph raised exact failure-step attribution by 4 to 10 points; no outside team has tested Chowdhury's propagate-by-code method, and no public protocol tests stale-state handling under all four conditions (Qian 2026).
agent_test: Record provenance (which claim depends on which check); on failure drop dependents by a deterministic pass, compare with asking the model per claim.

claim: Resetting the context to done-and-remaining while keeping environment state beat keeping full history (pass 0.52 vs 0.11 for full history and for restart, n=120).
agent_test: After a revision, rebuild the prompt from the ledger; compare with appending.

claim: Bayesian or confidence-weighted belief memory is inert when contradictions are rare (LoCoMo) and pays off only with a trustworthy per-claim reliability signal; content-inferred trust can be gamed and inverted confidence scores 0. Full text of the Singh paper now read: realistic macro 100 (reliability-weighted) vs 67 (last-write-wins) vs 46 (frequency) vs 90 (LLM over raw memory); a provenance-capped rule held attack success at 0% against 50 poison observations where last-write-wins reached 100%, but costs true corrections from low-tier sources (100% to 54%) and fails under laundering without taint tracking. Still one author and synthetic data.
agent_test: Weight claims by provenance (executed output vs model assertion), not by stated confidence.

claim: Agents rarely revise on refutation: across more than 25,000 runs evidence is ignored in 68% of traces and refutation-driven revision occurs in 26%; the base model explains 41.4% of variance, the scaffold 1.5%. The variance share does not show a scaffold cannot help, so the scaffold implication is contested.
agent_test: Same base model, scaffold with and without a forced Revise state, on tasks with a planted refutation.

claim: Tests that try to falsify beat confirming tests: in 12 LLMs on Wason-style games, confirmation bias predicts failure and reasoning models beat instruction-tuned ones (GPT-5.2-Chat 75% vs 33-41%).
agent_test: Require the agent to propose a check that would falsify the leading candidate before accepting it.

claim: Removing belief updating or replacing a failing hypothesis hurts a multi-step agent: MOIRA returns fall from 30.6% to 23.4% (no belief update) and to 2.8% (no reselection) for one model; more updates did not consistently help.
agent_test: Ablate the replace-failing-hypothesis step in the scaffold at equal tokens.

claim: Showing a model its prior assessment anchors the next one without making it more accurate (error up in 46.20% of cases, down in 30.28%); anti-anchoring prompts reduce the pull but not the error; a rule that keeps only evidence-backed revisions reduced harm at a coverage cost.
agent_test: Gate revision on a stated evidence item; measure harmful versus useful revisions.
audit_note: Zeng and Zhang: error up 46.20 / down 30.28 / unchanged 23.52 percent, anti-anchoring cut prior-directed shift but not error (it raised error; tested on Qwen3-8B only), evidence-validation rule traded coverage for reliability; DERELAB only corroborates anchoring generally (anchoring rates 0.43-0.48 for GPT-5.1 and Qwen3-32B).

claim: Direct tests of AGM or Darwiche-Pearl postulates on frontier LLMs exist only as an abstract-level workshop result (AGM-Bench: Success and Consistency satisfied, Inclusion and Preservation broken). No full numbers were verified. A second look at the page and OpenReview (HTTP 403) did not yield per-postulate numbers; the gap stays open.
agent_test: Run a small private postulate check (Inclusion, Preservation) on our agent's revise step.

claim: Explanation before dropping: only the Johnson-Laird lab shows that explaining a clash drives which belief people revise. Independent human studies (Elio and Pelletier 1997; Vasileiou et al. 2025) show the rule-first, non-minimal pattern but did not test explanation as a cause; Vasileiou found that giving an explanation still led to broad revision. No LLM study has tested explanation-first revision. In coding, an explanation step adds 0.4 to 2.8 points on top of unit-test feedback (Self-Debugging).
agent_test: A/B at equal tokens: one-line failure explanation before choosing the claim to drop vs direct drop. Count wrong-claim retentions. Do not expect more than a few points when real test output is already supplied.

claim: Error location is the limit on revision, and real execution output is what supplies it. Unit-test feedback lifted TransCoder 80.4 to 91.6 (Codex) and 77.3 to 88.8 (GPT-4); a human-written diagnosis lifted GPT-4 repair success from 33.3% to 52.6%; model-made hints lowered correction in 2 of 3 models (26.8 to 15.5, 29.1 to 12.8). Locating the faulty step in a long agent trace is hard: 48.9 to 52.7% exact on Who&When, 17.2% on trajectories of 33 to 130 steps; premise links raise step error identification by 6 to 16 points absolute.
agent_test: Measure how often the first-named culprit in the Revise state is the claim that actually caused the failure when the check is a test or stack trace vs a free-text critique. Roll back a flagged claim's dependents, not only the claim.
audit_note: Mukherjee et al. abstract reports premise-augmented step verification improving error identification by 6 to 16 percent absolute, not 3 to 14 points; other figures (TransCoder 80.4/77.3 to 91.6/88.8, 33.3 to 52.6, 26.8 to 15.5, 29.1 to 12.8, DeFA 48.9-52.7 and 17.2) check out.
claim_before_audit: Error location is the limit on revision, and real execution output is what supplies it. Unit-test feedback lifted TransCoder 80.4 to 91.6 (Codex) and 77.3 to 88.8 (GPT-4); a human-written diagnosis lifted GPT-4 repair success from 33.3% to 52.6%; model-made hints lowered correction in 2 of 3 models (26.8 to 15.5, 29.1 to 12.8). Locating the faulty step in a long agent trace is hard: 48.9 to 52.7% exact on Who&When, 17.2% on trajectories of 33 to 130 steps; premise links raise step error identification by 3 to 14 points.

claim: Pressure-driven flipping and evidence-driven updating share internal parts, so suppressing one by training or steering often damages the other. In four 3B to 8B models yielding to unsupported pushback was 17.1 to 73.6% and updating on valid evidence 53.7 to 64.1%; in one case (Llama-3.1, EX-FEVER) anti-pressure DPO cut yielding 32.9 points but cut rational updating 48.9 to 53.7 points; the correlation between sycophancy reduction and source-updating reduction was r=0.87 on four frontier 2026 models and 0.90 on open models. Source label and stated reliability change adoption (Claude Opus 5 vs Sonnet 5: 21% vs 78% user-claim adoption). The sources call for mitigations that decouple the two behaviors; placing the discrimination in the scaffold is a design inference, not a finding.
agent_test: Gate rule: a held claim may be changed only when the challenge carries new executed or retrieved evidence. Compare with an always-hold instruction and an always-update default on planted-defeater items and on bare 'are you sure' items together.
audit_note: Numbers verified (Ma: yielding 17.1-73.6, updating 53.7-64.1, Llama-3.1 EX-FEVER -32.9 vs -48.9/-53.7; Shapira: r=0.87 frontier and 0.90 open, Opus 5 21 vs Sonnet 5 78); but the trade-off is 'often' not always (Ma's orthogonalized steering gave modest selectivity gains, and the -32.9/-48.9..-53.7 figures are one Llama-3.1 EX-FEVER case), and 'discrimination should sit in the scaffold, not the weights' is the researcher's inference, not a finding; the sources call for mitigations that decouple the two behaviors.
claim_before_audit: Pressure-driven flipping and evidence-driven updating share internal parts, so suppressing one by training or steering damages the other. In four 3B to 8B models yielding to unsupported pushback was 17.1 to 73.6% and updating on valid evidence 53.7 to 64.1%; anti-pressure DPO cut yielding 32.9 points but cut rational updating 48.9 to 53.7 points; the correlation between sycophancy reduction and source-updating reduction was r=0.87 on four frontier 2026 models and 0.90 on open models. Source label and stated reliability change adoption (Claude Opus 5 vs Sonnet 5: 21% vs 78% user-claim adoption). So the discrimination should sit in the scaffold, not the weights.

claim: A one-line provenance rule works in agents with tools: two 2026 coding agents followed a stale instruction file over the actual code in 90.1% of 720 choices (code 4.2%), although Claude Code named the conflict in 79 of 80 runs; adding one sentence (follow the code when the two disagree) gave 91.4% code-matching and all 160 runs passed tests (vs 89.4%). It is a prompt rule, not a staged Revise state, and there is no equal-token comparison.
agent_test: Add the sentence 'executed output and the code outrank written notes and your own earlier statements' to S5 and test on tasks with a planted stale note; then test a full candidate-list Revise state against that sentence alone at equal tokens.

claim: Repeated failed revisions tend to loop. With complete verifier feedback, 78.7 to 90.2% of failed text-revision runs repeated an earlier output and 57.6 to 79.5% ended in a fixed point or cycle (19 models, 27,360 trajectories); prior recurrence cut later recovery (adjusted odds ratio 0.047). Clearing history at a recurrent state raised next-step escape by 42.2 and 49.2 points but final success only by 10.8 and 5.0. Whether lexicographic or restrained iterated revision oscillates less in an agent loop is still untested; only theory exists.
agent_test: Log whether the same claim is re-proposed after the same failed check; after two repeats force a different candidate or a reset. Compare with unlimited retries at equal tokens.

claim: Which entrenchment signal works is compared head to head in only one synthetic study. Recency (last-write-wins) scored 67 and frequency 46 on realistic regimes, reliability read from wording 100, and wording-based reliability scored 0 when confidence was inverted. Provenance-capped trust held poison success at 0% across 1 to 50 injected observations where recency and content-trust reached 100%, at the cost of blocking true corrections from low-tier sources (100% to 54%). No study compares executed-output provenance, stated confidence, recency and dependent count on a free-running LLM agent.
agent_test: Rank candidate claims by (1) came from executed output, (2) number of independent supports, (3) recency; use stated confidence only to break ties. Compare with rankings by confidence alone and recency alone on planted-defeater items.

claim: Published memory-framework scores for belief handling cannot yet be trusted across papers. The LoCoMo LLM judge is reported (secondhand) to accept up to 63% of wrong answers and about 6.4% of ground-truth answers contain errors; the same outputs scored 59.97 by a generous judge and 32.45 by strict token-F1. No independent reproduction of Kumiho, CUPMem, MOIRA or TOKI numbers was found. Typed-provenance guardrails (He and Yu) were checked only on 24 hand-written cases, not on a model.
agent_test: Score any memory or revise gain with a strict, answer-matching metric on a set with real contradictions; do not rely on a published LLM-judge number.
